Yifan Luo, Takafumi Matsumaru, Vibekananda Dutta, Xin He
This paper presents DPGS-SLAM (Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM) for dense mapping in environments containing dynamic objects. Objects in dynamic motion remain a significant challenge for dense visual SLAM since dynamic observations can contaminate camera tracking and scene reconstruction. Although 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) enables efficient dense mapping, existing 3DGS-SLAM systems may exhibit instability when dynamic objects violate their underlying static-scene assumption. Excluding dynamic observations can reduce their influence on tracking and mapping, but may leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained. Our proposed DPGS-SLAM is a monocular RGB SLAM framework that supports provisional representations of insufficiently observed static backgrounds through asynchronous diffusion-based background completion and provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Dynamic regions are identified through optical-flow-based motion discovery and temporally consistent mask propagation by SAM2. For selected keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance in occluded regions, while metric depth predicted from completed images initializes provisional Gaussian primitives. Provenance labels distinguish generated primitives from observation-supported primitives, excluding generated content from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are removed, and observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. Experimental results demonstrated competitive camera tracking, with average ATE RMSE values of 1.2 cm on TUM RGB-D and 2.7 cm on BONN RGB-D datasets. On StaDy4D, DPGS-SLAM improved average PSNR by 4.60 dB over WildGS-SLAM using only monocular RGB input.
♻ ☆ Learning to Live: A Step Toward Lifelong Embodied Intelligence
Lirong Che, Peidong Wang, Yimeng Su, Jiong Wang, Yang Chen, Wenbo Fu, Zhenyu Huang, Tiancheng Xu, Xueqian Wang, Yuzhe Yang, Dongli Xie, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Daqi Liu, Jian Su
Embodied agents are usually organized around individual tasks, yet the physical world keeps changing between tasks and during execution. We introduce LIFE (Lifelong Intelligence from Experience), a framework in which a robot observes continuously, remembers selectively, and turns experience into new capabilities. RoboBeats, a family of lightweight streaming gates, tracks conditions set by the agent and discovers new events, deciding when an observation warrants a response or a memory write. Selected observations enter Plastic Memory, a flat store of images and structured records that keeps the source evidence, so new fields and indexes can be added when later questions need them. When existing tools fall short, Explore-Distill-Mount (EDM) turns solutions found during problem solving into validated, reusable tools and skills. Under matched protocols, RoboBeats substantially improves condition tracking over its base models and, at the same writing budget, retains more useful evidence for memory question answering than uniform sampling. A case study of limited scale, replaying 24 hours of continuous video recorded by a real robot, illustrates how the integrated system builds memory from a day of experience and uses it to answer everyday questions. LIFE takes a step toward robots that become more familiar with their surroundings and more capable through experience: learning not only to complete tasks, but to live in the world.

Anticipating how future observations evolve along the instructed route provides predictive guidance beyond the current field of view, motivating video-action models (VAMs) that learn representations of future visual states. However, many existing VAMs couple future visual prediction with action generation during inference, despite their distinct temporal requirements: instruction-conditioned route guidance can be reused across multiple control steps, whereas local trajectories must continuously adapt to fresh observations. To bridge this gap, we introduce HAVANA, a dual-system VAM that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning. A slow system produces a compact language-conditioned latent plan from observation history, while a fast system combines the latest plan with the current observation to generate local trajectories. Their asynchronous execution enables rapid adaptation without repeated future prediction, and no future video is generated during inference. Experiments on OmniNavBench demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance over prior baselines, while zero-shot real-world deployments further show robust generalization to unseen environments.

♻ ☆ A Tactile-Informed Bi-Level Framework with Complementary Motion-Contact Planning and Tracking for Robust Model-Based In-Hand Manipulation
Yongpeng Jiang, Mingrui Yu, Yi Ren, Xiang Li
In dexterous in-hand manipulation, learning-based methods achieve strong task performance with increasing generalization to unseen objects. A complementary advantage of model-based methods, central to this work, is online adaptation to new task specifications without policy retraining, given suitable system models. However, due to the complexity of physical contacts and limited sensing modalities, existing model-based methods still struggle with modeling errors, even when using advanced contact models or optimization schemes, which limit their real-world applications. To advance the effectiveness and robustness of model-based contact-rich in-hand manipulation, this paper proposes a novel bi-level framework with tactile incorporation to mitigate these limitations. Specifically, at the high level, reference finger motions and contacts are jointly generated via contact-implicit model predictive control. The high-level module enables online reactive planning and disturbance recovery. At the low level, these references are concurrently tracked through a hand force-motion model and tactile feedback. The low-level module compensates for modeling errors and enhances manipulation robustness. The complementarity between the two levels is manifested in two dimensions: 1) subsystem decomposition, with a slow optimization-based planning layer and a fast tactile-reactive control layer; and 2) functional decomposition, combining task-level optimality with contact-level stability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing model-based methods in accuracy and robustness, while supporting online replanning during execution. Our method successfully completes a diverse set of challenging tasks in real-world environments, even under appreciable external disturbances and modeling uncertainties.

♻ ☆ Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids (DASH): Latency-Agnostic Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models for Humanoid Manipulation

Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.

☆ A Matching Lower Bound for Online Smooth Calibration
Kaixuan Ji, Quanquan Gu
We study smooth calibration error in sequential binary prediction, which measures how far a sequence of probabilistic forecasts is from being calibrated and, unlike the classical expected calibration error, is robust to small perturbations of the forecasts. Against adaptive adversaries, the minimax smooth calibration error is known to lie between $Ω(T^{1/3})$ and $O(\sqrt{T})$ (Qiao and Zheng, 2024), where $T$ is the number of rounds. In this paper, we close this gap by constructing a new adversary whose outcome mean moves with the forecaster's cumulative residual. This design makes compensating for past residuals costly, and forces every forecaster to incur an expected smooth calibration error of $Ω(\sqrt{T})$. This lower bound matches the known upper bound up to universal constants, and further implies $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ lower bounds for calibration distance and lower calibration distance. Overall, our results settle the minimax rates of these calibration measures in sequential prediction. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.
☆ Your PID Is Already a Neural Network: Learning Its Gains with Only Three Weights and No Teacher
Felipe de Jesús Félix-Arredondo, Nezih Nieto-Gutiérrez, Carlos Astengo-Noguez, Alejandro Ucan-Puc
A discrete PID controller is exactly a recurrent neural network, a classical state-space fact: a fixed linear memory of the running integral and the last error, read out by three trainable weights that map one-to-one to the PID gains. Networks with bounded hidden states, such as LSTMs of any width, only approximate it. Trained only on a one-step physical cost (the expected cost of one transition from a fixed state distribution), with no demonstrations, teacher controller, or known gains, the network solves a strongly convex least-squares problem, so gradient descent converges from any initialization to the unique one-step optimal PID gains; the limit network is that PID, with the same action on every error sequence. Partitioned regression then shows what extra capacity buys. Orthogonal residual features keep these gains and improve on the PID if and only if they correlate with the part of the optimal action outside the PID span. On a nonlinear second-order example the gap is 5.88% of the optimal PID cost, and 4.00% against PID with a bias; no controller can improve on PID by more on this objective. A residual started at a tuned PID begins exactly at that PID; at the one-step optimal PID, a fixed-feature residual's first gradient step lowers the cost if and only if its features can improve on the PID. Experiments confirm the realization, recovery, and gap results to numerical precision. On held-out plants of three families, under a protocol frozen before the test data existed, a residual warm-started at a heavily tuned PID and trained with it lowers the long-horizon cost by 3.5%, 3.5%, and 1.9%, with family-wise 95% bounds excluding zero, also under distribution shift; a post hoc comparison with the PID tuned alone suggests that most of it comes from the recurrent part in two families. The primary endpoint, a gain of at least 5% from a generic PID start, is not met in any family.

☆ Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation as an Optimization Constraint for Continual Learning
Davide Wiest
Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is a widely used regularization-based technique for continual learning, protecting performance on old tasks with a quadratic penalty whose empirical Fisher is usually justified through probabilistic curvature. We instead introduce Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC): new training must preserve chosen functionals of learned behavior. EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each sample's loss. This derivation exposes a flaw: EWC implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance. EWC-DR observed this failure in classification; CLOC identifies its general cause. Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation (IEWC) penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing the weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07).

☆ Characterizing the Edge of Stability in Variational Training Without Priors NeurIPS 2026
Juraj Marusic, Jonathan Wenger, Beau Coker, John P. Cunningham
Variational approaches in deep learning promise to deliver improved uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution generalization by inferring a distribution over weights, regularized by a divergence to a chosen prior. However, prior elicitation presents a significant challenge in deep learning, resulting in the common practice of significantly downweighting the regularization term in the variational objective. Recently, it was proposed to train solely via the expected loss by relying on implicit regularization from the optimizer, rather than explicit regularization from the divergence to the prior. While this approach largely sidesteps the issue of prior elicitation, current theory lacks an understanding of how key optimization hyperparameters impact the implicit regularization. Here, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that larger learning rates and fewer parameter samples lead to flatter minima of the loss landscape, which are known to generalize better. We show that training on the expected loss operates at a modified edge of stability, characterized by the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient estimates and the number of Monte Carlo samples. Experiments on out-of-distribution benchmark datasets confirm the practical significance of the theoretical results.

☆ Training Calibrated Conditional Generative Models with a Sample-Only Coverage Loss
Benjamin Remy, Raphael Rossellini, Chihway Chang, Rebecca Willett
Conditional generative models have become the tool of choice for sampling posteriors in scientific inverse problems, where we seek to sample images or signals conditioned on a set of indirect and noisy measurements. Yet they are often overconfident, which is a critical failure in scientific applications where accurate uncertainty quantification is essential. Existing regularizers fall short in complementary ways: differentiable coverage objectives require the model's density and do not identify the posterior, while strictly proper scoring rules such as the energy score need only samples but do not directly enforce coverage. We close this gap by introducing a differentiable loss function based on the expected coverage probability, estimated from samples alone. It applies to any conditional generative model, with no need for tractable densities or architectural changes. We prove that it is a strict divergence, vanishing if and only if the model equals the true posterior. On simulation-based inference benchmarks, it matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density. On high-dimensional imaging inverse problems, it yields better-calibrated posteriors than scoring-rule regularizers, with little change in the reconstruction quality of point estimates.

☆ A Latent Semiparametric Mixture Model for Robust Heterogeneity Learning in High Dimensions
Lyuou Zhang, Boxiang Wang, Lulu Wang, Wen Zhou, Hui Zou
Learning heterogeneity from high-dimensional data has become a fundamental task across many data-driven fields. Cluster analysis is a widely used unsupervised tool for this purpose, and many existing methods have been adapted to high-dimensional settings through sparsity constraints. In contrast to algorithmic approaches, model-based clustering offers clean theoretical guaranties and computational simplicity, but can be restrictive in practice due to its reliance on specific parametric distributions. We propose a novel latent semiparametric mixture model for clustering, in which the observed data follow a Gaussian mixture after latent coordinate-wise monotone transformations. Furthermore, assuming a sparse optimal clustering rule in the latent space, we develop a new method, CESME, tailored for high-dimensional clustering. By allowing unspecified transformations, our framework becomes substantially more flexible and robust than traditional model-based approaches. The clustering error of CESME is shown to approach the optimal clustering error at a rate matching that obtained when the true transformations are known. Extensive simulations and real data analysis confirm that CESME outperforms a broad range of existing high-dimensional clustering methods, including those designed for single-cell RNA sequencing data. The online supplementary file contains technical proofs, additional discussions, and more numerical results.

On twenty UCR datasets, GL-FRF improved on a tuned full-curve forest with the same number of trees on 16, with Brier score reductions of up to 0.21, significantly after Holm adjustment. No method was best on more than six datasets. ☆ From Link Prediction to Linear Community Detection: A Finite-Sample Guarantee for Graph Pretraining NeurIPS 2026
Ying Chen, Zhangyang Wang, Yixuan He
Link prediction (LP) is a standard pretraining objective for graph neural networks (GNNs): hide edges, train an encoder-decoder to predict them, and reuse the node embeddings for downstream node tasks. Despite its empirical success, there is little quantitative theory explaining why an edge-level objective should produce embeddings that are linearly useful for node classification. For any bounded GNN encoder paired with a symmetric bilinear decoder, we prove a conditional reduction: small population held-out LP excess risk implies small community-classification error for a transductive linear classifier on the learned embeddings. The bound decomposes into an optimization residual, an architectural approximation residual, and explicit statistical terms of order $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d/n})$ in bounded dense regimes. We further give a constructive few-label classifier: nearest-centroid classification under the positive semidefinite quadratic form $G = W Z^\top Z W$, whose label error is coupled to LP quality. The framework is architecture-agnostic through the approximation residual, and we instantiate this residual as $O(\log n / n)$ for a graph isomorphism network (GIN) with spectral positional encoding and a bilinear decoder. Synthetic SBM experiments validate the theorem chain from LP risk to score error to classification error, and show when the worst-case constants become conservative.

☆ Conformal prediction for censored life history data

We consider individual prediction of general summaries of a multistate trajectory, such as time alive out of hospital or time spent in remission. We weight observed coverage decisions by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored to that time and augment the estimator with conditional coverage probabilities for unresolved histories. For a fixed region, the coverage estimator is doubly robust with respect to the censoring and conditional coverage models and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound when both are consistent at suitable rates. For the calibrated region, we derive a finite-sample lower bound on the coverage probability and establish asymptotic validity if either model is correct. In simulations, using partial histories yields narrower prediction intervals at comparable coverage. We illustrate joint prediction of days in and out of hospital in the HF-ACTION trial and prediction of relapse-free time in the German Breast Cancer Study Group cohort.

♻ ☆ There Will Be a Scientific Theory of Deep Learning
Jamie Simon, Daniel Kunin, Alexander Atanasov, Enric Boix-Adserà, Blake Bordelon, Jeremy Cohen, Nikhil Ghosh, Florentin Guth, Arthur Jacot, Mason Kamb, Dhruva Karkada, Eric J. Michaud, Berkan Ottlik, Joseph Turnbull
In this paper, we make the case that a scientific theory of deep learning is emerging. By this we mean a theory which characterizes important properties and statistics of the training process, hidden representations, final weights, and performance of neural networks. We pull together major strands of ongoing research in deep learning theory and identify five growing bodies of work that point toward such a theory: (a) solvable idealized settings that provide intuition for learning dynamics in realistic systems; (b) tractable limits that reveal insights into fundamental learning phenomena; (c) simple mathematical laws that capture important macroscopic observables; (d) theories of hyperparameters that disentangle them from the rest of the training process, leaving simpler systems behind; and (e) universal behaviors shared across systems and settings which clarify which phenomena call for explanation. Taken together, these bodies of work share certain broad traits: they are concerned with the dynamics of the training process; they primarily seek to describe coarse aggregate statistics; and they emphasize falsifiable quantitative predictions. We argue that the emerging theory is best thought of as a mechanics of the learning process, and suggest the name learning mechanics. We discuss the relationship between this mechanics perspective and other approaches for building a theory of deep learning, including the statistical and information-theoretic perspectives. In particular, we anticipate a symbiotic relationship between learning mechanics and mechanistic interpretability. We also review and address common arguments that fundamental theory will not be possible or is not important. We conclude with a portrait of important open directions in learning mechanics and advice for beginners. We host further introductory materials, perspectives, and open questions at learningmechanics.pub.

Evolved features improve over single-shot rubrics by +2.9 pp on average and outperform zero-shot LLM classification on two of three tasks, while providing fully auditable decision logic. On the credit risk task, the zero-shot LLM performs at chance (50.7%) with a strong bias toward a single class, whereas evolved features achieve balanced, interpretable predictions. Crucially, this failure is invisible in aggregate accuracy and surfaces only under per-class auditing. Analysis reveals that evolution is most effective when label boundaries cannot be inferred from category names alone or when the LLM lacks reliable domain-specific reasoning.
♻ ☆ Quantum Geometry of Data
Alexander G. Abanov, Luca Candelori, Harold C. Steinacker, Martin T. Wells, Jerome R. Busemeyer, Cameron J. Hogan, Vahagn Kirakosyan, Nicola Marzari, Sunil Pinnamaneni, Dario Villani, Mengjia Xu, Kharen Musaelian
We demonstrate how Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML) encodes data as quantum geometry. In QCML, features of the data are represented by learned Hermitian matrices, and data points are mapped to states in Hilbert space. The quantum geometry description endows the dataset with rich geometric and topological structure---including intrinsic dimension, quantum metric, and Berry curvature---derived directly from the data. QCML captures global properties of data through a compact operator representation. At fixed Hilbert-space dimension, the number of operator parameters grows only linearly with the number of features. The present work provides the first full exposition of QCML as a framework for matrix geometry, establishing its mathematical foundation and demonstrating how operator-level tools from quantum geometry can be directly applied to data. We introduce the matrix Laplacian and its eigenmaps as a geometry-preserving alternative to graph-based embeddings, and we show how topological invariants such as Chern numbers can be extracted from data for the first time. An important practical outcome is the efficiency of the representation: the relevant geometric structure of high-dimensional datasets can be captured with Hilbert spaces of size as small as $N \sim 10$. We illustrate these results on a number of synthetic and real-world examples, including the Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset, where QCML uncovers geometric separability between benign and malignant samples and yields an interpretable decomposition of feature relevance. The emphasis of this work is on a new geometric representation of data rather than on algorithmic benchmarking, establishing a foundation for extracting global geometric and topological structure from high-dimensional datasets.
comment: 31 pages, 16 figures. Updated the Wisconsin Breast Cancer analysis, added a versioned repository reference, clarified the distinction between the response matrix and the quantum metric, and corrected formulas and simulation details
♻ ☆ Uniform-in-Time Weak Propagation-of-Chaos in Shallow Neural Networks
Margalit Glasgow, Joan Bruna
We consider one-hidden layer neural networks trained in the feature-learning regime using gradient descent, and relate the output of the finite-width network $f_{\hatρ_t^m}$ to its infinite-width counterpart $f_{ρ_t^{MF}}$, which evolves in the mean-field dynamics. While constant-time horizon bounds for $\|f_{ρ_t^{MF}} - f_{\hatρ_t^m}\|$ may be obtained via standard Grönwall estimates, the long-time behavior of the fluctuation is a more delicate matter. Uniform-in-time bounds often rely on (local) strong convexity in the landscape or Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities present in noisy gradient dynamics. In this work, we establish non-asymptotic weak propagation-of-chaos that holds uniformly in time, obtained by exploiting instead the convergence rate of the mean-field deterministic Wasserstein-gradient-flow dynamics. Specifically, denoting by $L_t$ the mean-field excess MSE loss at time $t$ and $m$ the number of neurons, under standard regularity assumptions and the condition $\int_0^\infty L_t^{1/2} dt =O(\log d)$, we obtain the uniform in time bound $\|f_{ρ_t^{MF}}- f_{\hatρ_t^m}\|^2 \lesssim \text{poly}(d) m^{-\min(1,c/6)}$ whenever $L_t \lesssim t^{-c}$. Our result holds in a noiseless setting and does not make any assumptions on the geometry of the landscape near the optimum, and extends seamlessly to other forms of discretization, including finite number of samples and time discretization. A key takeaway of our result is that whenever the convergence rate of the mean-field, population-loss dynamics is faster than $t^{-2}$, we can attain a loss of $ε$ with only $\text{poly}(d/ε)$ neurons, training samples, and GD steps.
comment: 52 pages
♻ ☆ Functional Stochastic Localization
Anming Gu, Bobby Shi, Kevin Tian
Eldan's stochastic localization is a probabilistic construction that has proved instrumental to modern breakthroughs in high-dimensional geometry and the design of sampling algorithms. Motivated by sampling under non-Euclidean geometries and the mirror descent algorithm in optimization, we develop a functional generalization of Eldan's process that replaces Gaussian regularization with regularization by any positive integer multiple of a log-Laplace transform. We further give a mixing time bound on the Markov chain induced by our localization process, which holds if our target distribution satisfies a functional Poincaré inequality. Finally, we apply our framework to differentially private convex optimization in $\ell_p$ norms for $p \in [1, 2)$, where we improve state-of-the-art query complexities in a zeroth-order model.
